parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Define half-life of a radioactive isotope.

markscheme_points.text: time for activity (of sample) to halve

hints: Hint 1: Think about which quantity you can actually measure getting smaller with time for a radioactive sample, such as its count rate or number of undecayed nuclei.
parts.proper_answer: The time taken for the activity of the sample to fall to half its initial value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Half Means in Decay**
You start with a large number of unstable nuclei. They decay at random, so the number left, $N$, and the activity, $A$, both fall with time. Half-life is simply the time for that measurable amount to become half as big.

Step 2: **Precise Definition**
So half-life $T_{1/2}$ is the time taken for half of the initially present unstable nuclei to decay, which is the same as the time for the activity $A$ to halve: $$A = \frac{A_0}{2} \text{ after time } T_{1/2}$$

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: State the name of the quantity represented by the magnitude of the gradient of line X in Fig. 9.1.
hints: Hint 1: On a graph of number of nuclei $N$ against time $t$, think about what the gradient $\Delta N / \Delta t$ physically means as a rate.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Gradient to Rate**
Line X shows $N$ falling with $t$. Its gradient is $$\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta t}$$ which is negative because $N$ is decreasing. Its magnitude tells you how many nuclei decay per second.

Step 2: **Recall Activity**
Activity $A$ is defined as the rate of decay: $$A = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$$ So the magnitude of the gradient of the $N$-$t$ graph at any time $t$ is exactly the activity of X at that time.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State three conclusions about X or Y that may be drawn from Fig. 9.1. The conclusions may be qualitative or quantitative. Use the space below for any working that you need.

markscheme_points.text: total number of nuclei is constant
amount (of X) at t = 0 is 0.066 mol
activity (of X) at t = 0 is 2.0 × 10^21 Bq

hints: Hint 1: Look at the long-term behaviour of curve Y and the sum $N_X + N_Y$ at several times, for example at $t = 0$, $14$ s and $40$ s.
Hint 2: Read off the starting number of X nuclei at $t = 0$ from Fig. 9.1, then find the time when this number has fallen to exactly half.
Hint 3: Think how you can turn the numbers you read off into other quantities, such as decay constant $\lambda = \ln 2 / T_{1/2}$, moles $= N / N_A$, or initial activity $A_0 = \lambda N_0$.
parts.proper_answer: Any three from: Y is stable (does not decay); total number $N_X + N_Y = 4.0 \times 10^{22}$ is constant; half-life of X is about $13$ to $14$ s; decay constant of X is about $0.051\text{ s}^{-1}$; initial amount of X is about $0.066\text{ mol}$; initial activity of X is about $2.0 \times 10^{21}\text{ Bq}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Happens to Y**
X falls from $4.0 \times 10^{22}$ to near zero while Y rises from zero to $4.0 \times 10^{22}$. Y keeps building up and never falls, so Y must be stable and not decay further.

Step 2: **Total Nuclei Stay Constant**
Pick any $t$. At $t = 0$, $N_X = 4.0 \times 10^{22}$, $N_Y = 0$. At the crossover near $t = 14$ s, $N_X = N_Y = 2.0 \times 10^{22}$. At $t = 40$ s, $N_X \approx 0.5 \times 10^{22}$, $N_Y \approx 3.5 \times 10^{22}$. In each case: $$N_X + N_Y = 4.0 \times 10^{22}$$ Every X that decays becomes one Y.

Step 3: **Half-Life and Decay Constant**
Initial $N_0 = 4.0 \times 10^{22}$. Half is $2.0 \times 10^{22}$, which is reached at $t \approx 13.6$ s. That is $T_{1/2}$. Then: $$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{13.6} \approx 0.051\text{ s}^{-1}$$ You could also quote initial moles $N_0/N_A \approx 0.066$ mol or initial activity $A_0 = \lambda N_0 \approx 2.0 \times 10^{21}$ Bq.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The mass of radioactive isotope X in the sample in (b) is $7.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{kg}$ at time $t = 0$.

Determine the nucleon number of isotope X.
hints: Hint 1: Start from Fig. 9.1 and read the total number of X nuclei present at $t = 0$, then think how total mass and number are related to mass of one nucleus.
Hint 2: Divide the given total mass $7.3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg}$ by that initial number to get the mass of a single X nucleus.
Hint 3: Recall that one nucleon has mass about $1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, so think how to convert mass of one nucleus into a count of nucleons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Mass of One Nucleus**
From Fig. 9.1 at $t = 0$: $$N_0 = 4.0 \times 10^{22}$$ Total mass is $m_{total} = 7.3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg}$. So one nucleus has mass: $$m_{nucleus} = \frac{m_{total}}{N_0} = \frac{7.3 \times 10^{-4}}{4.0 \times 10^{22}} \approx 1.83 \times 10^{-26}\text{ kg}$$

Step 2: **Convert Mass to Nucleon Number**
Each nucleon (proton or neutron) has mass about $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$. The nucleon number $A$ is how many such units make up the nucleus: $$A = \frac{m_{nucleus}}{u} = \frac{7.3 \times 10^{-4}}{4.0 \times 10^{22} \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}}$$

Step 3: **Calculate and Round to Integer**
Evaluating: $$A \approx \frac{1.825 \times 10^{-26}}{1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 11$$ Nucleon number must be a whole number, so $A = 11$.
